topic: LLM agents; procedural skills; benchmark methodology
status: cross-paper conditional synthesis; independent external replication required
claim: A current broad paired benchmark (SkillsBench v4: 87 tasks, eight domains, 18 model–harness configurations, three trials per cell) finds curated Skills raise mean task-macro pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 pp), but the lift ranges +4.1 to +25.7 pp across configurations and 13/87 tasks have negative deltas. A separate SkillAxe study on a different/older SkillsBench snapshot and one agent stack decomposes its native-score improvement (26.7% to 41.6%) entirely into increased task-output coverage; correctness among output-producing tasks stays 57.1%. On its held-out SpreadsheetBench common subset (N=50), SkillAxe and a larger LLM-self skill library both score 52%, while no-skill scores 16%, suggesting a library-size/activation benefit rather than an accuracy advantage there. Thus “skills improve agent performance” is supported only with task, quality, harness and metric qualifiers; unconditional correctness improvement is not established.

sources.title: SkillAxe: Sharpening LLM-Authored Agent Skills Through Evaluation-Guided Self-Refinement
locators: §4.1/Table 2: native score decomposition into coverage and conditional quality; SkillsBench older/different snapshot and one Claude Opus 4.5+Harbor setup
§4.3/Table 3: SpreadsheetBench held-out common N=50; 52% SkillAxe and LLM-self vs 16% no-skill

interpretation: Current SkillsBench v4 is strong evidence that selected high-quality procedural Skills often help in its evaluated stacks, but its 13 negative task deltas and quality-selection protocol limit universal transfer. SkillAxe suggests one mechanism is getting runnable outputs rather than improving answer quality; because its data version, harness and score differ, this is triangulation, not head-to-head replication. SoK 2602.20867 is not counted as an independent empirical study.
falsifiable_question: In a preregistered paired evaluation, do curated/refined skills improve correctness conditional on a completed output, or mainly raise completion coverage? Does the effect survive representative (not top-quartile) skill quality, separate human and deterministic verifiers, multiple model–harness stacks, and held-out task domains? Are complexity/applicability metadata plus a lightweight fallback enough to eliminate negative per-task effects without sacrificing average lift?
primary_outcome: Report per-task and macro completion coverage; correctness among completed outputs; joint end-to-end success; paired per-task deltas and negative-effect rate; wall-clock/token cost; results separately under deterministic and blinded human/fair grading.
counterevidence_and_caveats: SkillsBench v4 reports positive mean lift in every one of 18 tested configurations, supporting a real and broad benefit under curated benchmark conditions.
13/87 task-level negative deltas directly contradict a claim that every task benefits.
SkillsBench selected benchmark skills from the top quality quartile; it explicitly calls this optimistic relative to ecosystem skills.
SkillAxe's SkillsBench experiment uses a different/older snapshot, one model-harness stack and only two trials per task; it is not directly comparable to current SkillsBench v4.
SkillAxe's fair grader and some diagnostics use LLM judges; authors acknowledge calibration/positional bias and interactions among skills.
SpreadsheetBench's N=50 common subset is one deployment-oriented benchmark and does not establish general accuracy equivalence.
These are two primary empirical papers plus one sampled SoK context, not a representative meta-analysis; global novelty and broad real-world transfer are unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Freeze a task set and skill snapshot; preregister paired no-skill, expert-curated, LLM-self, and evaluation-refined arms. Sample skills across ecosystem quality rather than top quartile. Run at least three harness/model families and three seeds/trials per cell. Score every run first for output completion, then independently score semantic correctness among completed outputs using deterministic tests plus blinded human review. Report per-task deltas, negative-effect rate, coverage, conditional quality, joint success, tokens/time, and a separate held-out domain. Use validation-only skill refinement and keep test verifiers hidden.

topic: automated program repair; semantic transformation; generalization
status: single-study robust within-paper effect; independent datasets and replication needed
claim: In a sampled 2025 Java APR study, 11 open LLMs produced on average 49.48% fewer correct fixes and 42.90% fewer plausible fixes on semantics-preserving transformed Defects4J than on original Defects4J. On four selected weak generalizers, adding bug reports increased correct/plausible fixes by 111.72%/97.77% relative to their transformed-set two-shot baseline, yet 10 of 12 model/prompt setups still did not reach the original-set result. This supports a specific concern that benchmark scores can be representation-sensitive and that repair context helps without necessarily restoring generalization; it does not establish the same effect size on other languages, newer models, or naturally shifted bugs.

sources.title: Evaluating the Generalizability of LLMs in Automated Program Repair
locators: §III: semantics-preserving transformation of Defects4J and selection of 11 open models
Table II: 49.48%/42.90% mean decline in correct/plausible fixes
Table III and §IV-B: repair-context gains for four selected models; 10/12 setups remain below original baseline
§V: manual semantic review threat; §VI: Java-only and model-scope limitations

interpretation: This is a strong controlled representation-sensitivity result within one transformed benchmark lineage, not a natural-distribution-shift estimate. Transformed examples derive from the same 438 single-function Java defects; correctness adjudication involved manual patch review. Bug-report gain is relative to the transformed-set two-shot baseline, not a universal causal estimate.
falsifiable_question: Across independently collected post-cutoff Java and non-Java defects, does a preregistered suite of semantics-preserving identifier, control-flow and dead-code transformations reduce correct repair rates after matching difficulty and test strength? Does static/dynamic semantic normalization recover repair success on held-out projects without leaking bug labels or patch templates?
primary_outcome: Correct fixes under hidden regression tests plus blinded semantic review; plausible fixes separately; report original/transformed paired effect per transformation family, project-held-out confidence intervals, and performance with bug reports/fault localization selected without test leakage.
counterevidence_and_caveats: All 11 studied models declined on transformed Defects4J, making the within-paper direction consistent.
Repair-relevant context yielded substantial gains for four selected models; the result is not simply ‘prompts do not help.’
Only 11 open models up to 34B and Java were tested; results may not transfer to contemporary closed models or other languages.
The transformed set is derived from the original 438 single-function bugs and does not estimate naturally occurring distribution shift.
Semantic correctness of plausible patches was manually adjudicated, an acknowledged internal-validity risk, although released patch data supports replication.
No independent replication or cross-dataset estimate was completed in this batch; global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Replicate the published protocol, then preregister held-out projects/languages and transformation families. Keep transformed variants paired with originals, manually validate semantic preservation on a blinded sample, add independently collected post-cutoff bugs, and separate model selection from test evaluation. Compare prompts with bug reports, fault localization, tests, and combinations under matched inference budgets; report correct/plausible fixes and per-project uncertainty.

topic: automated program repair; metamorphic testing; benchmark familiarity
status: two-study convergence with cross-dataset counterexample; causal mechanism unsettled
claim: Two independent 2025–2026 APR studies find repair behavior sensitive to semantics-preserving code transformations on Defects4J, but their effects are not a universal constant. One study reports a large 49.48% mean decline in correct-fix counts across 11 open models on transformed Defects4J. A second reports significant 4.01–15.98 percentage-point success-rate declines across seven models on transformed Defects4J among bugs solvable in their original form. On newer GitBug-Java, however, GPT-4o and Claude-3.7 show no significant mean decline, and GPT-4o-mini's −8.67-point result is not significant (p=.074), despite large regressions on individual bugs. The second study finds some association with model NLL/familiarity but also an inverted-U pattern for several open models. The defensible synthesis is transformation-sensitive behavior on historical benchmarks with meaningful model/task heterogeneity—not proof that all benchmark success is memorization.

sources.title: A Metamorphic Testing Approach to Diagnosing Memorization in LLM-Based Program Repair
locators: §3: Defects4J and GitBug-Java, natural transformations, ten prompts per version
§4.1/Table 2: significant drops on Defects4J among originally solvable bugs
§4.1: no significant average drop for GPT-4o/Claude-3.7 on GitBug-Java; smaller solvable sample
§4.2: NLL relationship including inverted-U result for some open models; NLL is proxy

interpretation: The two studies use different models, success definitions, prompt budgets and denominators, so the numerical effect sizes should not be pooled. The second study's GitBug-Java result is counterevidence to uniform average drops, while low statistical power and per-bug failures prevent treating it as proof of invariance. NLL supports a familiarity association but cannot establish exposure or causal memorization.
falsifiable_question: Under a shared preregistered protocol, do transformed-input repair losses differ between older and post-cutoff bugs after matching original solvability, project, patch count and model? Does NLL predict transformation sensitivity out of sample beyond bug difficulty and code complexity, and do its predictions remain monotonic across models?
primary_outcome: Paired per-bug transformed-minus-original rate of human-verified correct patches, with test-adequate patches reported separately; stratify by benchmark vintage, original solvability, transformation family and model. Report confidence intervals, individual severe regressions, NLL calibration and sample power.
counterevidence_and_caveats: Both studies independently report transformation sensitivity on Defects4J, supporting reproducibility of the direction in that benchmark lineage.
The newer study does not find significant mean declines for two closed models on GitBug-Java; this limits a universal claim.
The GitBug-Java originally-solvable subset is small, so null results may be underpowered; individual bug regressions remain large.
The 2025 study reports fix counts; the 2026 study reports per-bug prompt success rates among originally solvable bugs, so effects are not directly comparable.
The 2026 study uses test-adequate patches as its large-scale outcome; passing tests does not guarantee semantic correctness.
NLL is a proxy for familiarity and is unavailable for closed models; it is not direct evidence of training-data exposure.
Only Java function-level APR was audited; global novelty and transfer are unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Use common model versions and prompts on historical Defects4J plus time-stamped post-cutoff bugs. Match bugs on original passability and project, apply human-validated natural transformations, fix candidate count and inference budget, and independently adjudicate a stratified sample of patches. Preregister NLL-by-difficulty interactions; use held-out projects for calibration and report null and worst-case results.
